hero.name: Hari
hero.who: a retired post office clerk in Kolkata whose days get ruined by small annoyances

story.b: Hari retired from the post office last year, and he imagined calm mornings with tea and the newspaper. Instead, small things keep spoiling his days. The milkman comes late. The 7:40 bus to the market skips his stop. A young man on the tram pushes past without a word, and Hari grumbles about it until lunch. When his daughter-in-law forgets to save him a piece of fish, he sulks through dinner. One evening his old friend Bimal, sitting beside him on the bench near the pond, asks how retirement is going. Hari starts listing every irritation of the week. Halfway through, he notices Bimal smiling. Hari realises he has spent a whole week angry about things that lasted a few seconds each.

ask.q: Hari spends whole days angry about tiny events. What is the most useful first step for him?
o: Avoid the bus, the tram and anything else that might annoy him
Notice that the long anger comes from how he reads each event
Complain to his family so they stop causing these problems
ask.why: Avoiding every annoyance is impossible in a busy city, and asking others to change only hands them his peace. The events themselves last seconds. What stretches them into a whole day is the meaning he adds, and that part is in his hands.

chapters.take: Small events last seconds. Our grumbling about them can last all day.

story.h: The neighbour who did not wave
story.b: On Sunday morning Hari waves to Mr Ghosh from the balcony, and Mr Ghosh walks on without waving back. Hari's chest tightens at once. He must still be upset about the parking argument, Hari thinks. By the time his tea is cold, he has built a whole story of insult. Then he tries something new. He takes the back page of his old diary and writes only what happened. A man walked past. He did not wave. That is all. Seen like that, it looks small and a little silly. In the afternoon he meets Mr Ghosh at the sweet shop. Mr Ghosh says he left his glasses at home and could barely see the road.

ask.q: Next time something like this upsets him, what should Hari do first?
o: Write down the plain facts and notice which parts he added himself
Confront the person at once so the matter is cleared up
Ignore his feelings and pretend nothing bothered him
ask.why: Writing the plain facts separates what happened from the story he told himself, and the story is where the pain lives. Rushing to confront someone acts on that story before checking it. Pretending nothing happened just pushes the feeling down, where it keeps working.

chapters.take: Separate what happened from what you told yourself about it.

story.b: Every November, Hari must visit the bank to prove he is alive so his pension continues. This year he reaches at ten, and the clerk says the server is down. Come back after lunch, maybe. The man behind Hari starts shouting. Hari feels the same heat rising in himself. Then he takes out a small notebook and makes two quick lists. Not mine: the server, the clerk's mood, the crowd. Mine: having my papers in order, coming back calmly, how I spend the next three hours. He walks to the library across the road, reads two chapters of a detective novel and eats a plate of ghugni. At two o'clock the server is working. Hari is fourth in line, and still in a good mood.

ask.q: The man behind Hari is still shouting at the counter. What would be the most helpful thing for Hari to tell him?
o: Shout together, so the bank fixes the server faster
Write a long complaint now, since the day is ruined anyway
Keep his papers ready and use the wait well, since the server is not his to fix
ask.why: Shouting does not repair a server, and treating the day as ruined gives one fault power over the whole afternoon. Sorting out what is his, his papers, his calm and his free hours, puts his energy where it can actually change something.

chapters.take: Put your energy into your own choices, not into things you cannot steer.

story.b: The housing society meets on Saturday to discuss repairing the water tank, and Hari knows Mr Dutta will be there. Mr Dutta interrupts everyone, mocks every idea and calls the older members slow. Last time Hari left shaking with anger. This time, over his morning tea, Hari prepares. He tells himself that Mr Dutta will probably be rude, and that this says more about Mr Dutta's own worries than about anyone else. He decides on three things. He will speak once, clearly. He will not raise his voice. He will thank people who help. At the meeting Mr Dutta calls his tank plan childish. Hari nods, explains the cost again and asks for a vote. The plan passes. Hari walks home feeling light.

ask.q: Bimal dreads a family wedding where one cousin always makes nasty remarks. What should Bimal do?
o: Skip the wedding so he does not have to face the cousin
Expect the remarks and decide beforehand how to stay polite and firm
Prepare sharp replies so he can win this time
ask.why: Skipping the wedding lets one cousin take away a family celebration. Sharp replies turn it into a battle he will keep replaying. Expecting the remarks removes the shock, and deciding in advance how to respond means he stays kind and steady on his own terms.

chapters.take: Expect difficult people, and decide in advance how you will stay kind.

story.b: Hari's younger brother Shankar forgot to call on his birthday, and Hari has been punishing him with silence for two weeks. Every time Shankar's name flashes on his phone, Hari lets it ring. One rainy afternoon he pulls out the family photo album to show his granddaughter. There is a picture from 1987 of the two brothers at a cousin's wedding, refusing to stand together because of some fight. Hari cannot even remember what the fight was about. His granddaughter laughs at their sulking faces. Hari laughs too, then goes quiet. He asks himself whether a missed phone call will matter to anyone a year from now. That evening, when Shankar calls again, Hari picks up and talks for forty minutes.

ask.q: Hari's daughter-in-law is still upset about a week-old argument with her sister. What gentle advice could Hari offer?
o: Ask whether it will matter a year from now, and let the small part go
Wait for her sister to apologise first, however long it takes
Bring the argument up again until everyone agrees who was right
ask.why: Waiting for an apology can stretch a small hurt into months of distance. Reopening the fight to prove a point usually makes it bigger. Looking at it from a year away shows how little it weighs, which makes it easier to drop and enjoy the people still around her.

chapters.take: Ask if today's worry will matter in a year. Most will not.

story.b: After the tank meeting, the society asks Hari to keep its accounts for a year. It is dull work. Every evening he sits at the dining table with a ledger, a calculator and a cup of tea, entering maintenance payments and plumber bills. Nobody thanks him. Once, Mr Dutta even suggests the numbers look odd. The old Hari would have resigned in a huff. Instead he double-checks every receipt, writes each entry neatly and pins a clear summary on the notice board near the lift. He reminds himself that the job is simply to do this page well, then the next one. One evening the watchman's daughter asks how he balances the columns. Hari spends half an hour teaching her, and enjoys it more than any praise.

ask.q: Hari's treasurer work gets no thanks and one unfair doubt. What is the wisest way for him to carry on?
o: Do it less carefully, since nobody notices the effort anyway
Resign and let someone who wants praise take over
Keep doing each entry honestly and well, whether or not anyone thanks him
ask.why: Doing it carelessly or quitting both hand control to other people's reactions. The work still matters to the families who pay maintenance. Giving full care to the task in front of him, without waiting for applause, is what builds his character and keeps him steady.

chapters.take: Do the task in front of you well, and let the applause be optional.

story.b: By the time the winter sun turns soft, Hari's days feel different. The bus still skips his stop sometimes. The milkman is still late. Mr Dutta still interrupts. But Hari now walks to the next stop and buys peanuts on the way. He writes the plain facts when something stings, and most of it fades before lunch. Shankar comes over for Sunday lunch, and the brothers argue happily about football. The society accounts are balanced and pinned up every month. One evening on the bench by the pond, Bimal asks again how retirement is going. Hari thinks for a moment, then talks about the watchman's daughter, who now checks his columns for him. He forgets to mention a single complaint.

chapters.take: Calm is not a quiet life. It is a quieter way of reading it.
